text: Calculus is an unlikely engine for a film, and this one runs on it for a hundred and three minutes. Ramón Menéndez puts a mathematics teacher, Jaime Escalante, in front of a class the school has already sorted into its low column, and the drama comes from the ordinary machinery of instruction: drills, homework, hours nobody is paid for. What stands to be lost is not affection but arithmetic — whether teenagers written off as gang members and no-hopers can be brought, inside a single year, to work the institution around them does not expect and may be slow to credit. A Best Actor citation attaches to the man at the blackboard. The National Film Registry took the picture in later, an odd afterlife for a story about homework.

A girl cuts her hair and takes a boy's name so that she will be allowed to read. The prohibition is the whole architecture: scripture is closed to women, so study has to be conducted as a disguise, and every hour of learning gets paid for with a lie told at close range to people who have started to like her. Barbra Streisand directs it and sings it, which is a stranger decision than it looks — the songs are private, sung by someone who cannot say aloud what she is, so the numbers carry a confession the dialogue is not permitted to make. Two of its three Academy honors went to how the film sounds and how it was built, the song score and the production design; a third went to supporting work. What is risked is not exposure alone but the loss of the one room she talked her way into.

Roman soldiers throw dice for a dead man's clothing, and the winner finds he cannot afterward put the garment down. The Robe assembles two and a quarter hours of historical spectacle out of an object and a bad conscience: Marcellus Gallio, drunk, unbelieving, chasing his own slave across the empire on the theory that destroying the thing will quiet him. Henry Koster shoots at scale and in color, and the Academy honors went where the budget is visible, cinematography and art direction, with a third for the lead. The pressure, though, is smaller than the sets. A man raised to regard executions as ordinary administrative work is being asked, by symptoms he cannot account for, to consider that one of them was not ordinary at all.

A Soviet submarine runs aground on a sandbar within sight of a New England summer colony. The problem is mechanical and entirely fixable; the danger is that the islanders will notice. Norman Jewison plays it as farce — a lieutenant named Rozanov sent ashore to borrow help, insisting to everyone who asks that he and his men are Norwegian, while a police chief and a vacationing television writer try to work out how frightened they ought to be. Two hours of comedy resting on a fear that was not funny in 1966, which was the wager. Three Academy honors, Best Picture among them, indicate how the wager was read at the time. The subject is panic rather than politics: how fast a small place can talk itself into an invasion.

The job is offered as a rescue: a housemaid's place with a good family in the 1930s South, taken by a young woman so she will not have to earn her living another way. That framing puts everyone in the house in the position of a benefactor with opinions. Told flatly, the story blames Rose for the trouble that follows; Martha Coolidge is more interested in the adults deciding what her wanting means and who is entitled to rule on it. The register stays domestic — porches, kitchens, a doctor's household with settled ideas about propriety — so pressure gathers in conversation rather than incident. Both Academy acting honors here went to women. What stands to be lost is a family's ability to go on thinking of itself as kind.

Three hours and five minutes is a long time to spend inside one man's obedience. Otto Preminger uses the length for scale rather than incident: a Boston priest climbs an institution across decades in which bigotry at home and Nazism abroad keep arriving as matters the Church will either answer for or decline to. The Academy honors were for surfaces, color cinematography and art direction and costume, and that is not incidental. Vestments, marble, the choreography of a procession: the visible apparatus of office is what a man is being fitted into, and his private conflicts get measured against it. What the running time keeps circling is whether a career of correct decisions inside a hierarchy amounts to a life a person would have chosen.

Two American soldiers spend the First World War escaping, and most of their energy goes into annoying each other. Lewis Milestone shot it in 1927: ninety-two minutes of pursuit that begins with Germans in the field and ends up somewhere considerably warmer, the rivalry over a woman functioning mainly as one more thing the pair can lose to. Its prize was called Best Director, Comedy Picture — a category name that records how differently the industry once sorted its own product. The Academy Film Archive preserved the film in 2016 with the University of Nevada, Las Vegas Foundation. Slapstick does not usually attract that sort of custodianship, and the physical survival of a joke is an argument of its own.

The scandal is the plot: Lady Hamilton, Admiral Horatio Nelson, and an empire obliged to have an opinion about the pair of them. Frank Lloyd's 1929 picture treats a love affair as a matter of state, which is accurate to the situation — one of the two is an instrument of the navy, and his reputation is national property. Ninety-nine minutes is not much for a history, so the film spends it on proximity rather than campaigns: rooms, receptions, the management of what other people are permitted to see. Nothing between them stays private, because privacy is not available to either of them. Academy honors went to the direction, the lead actress, and the camera. That distribution says where the weight of the thing sits, and it is not on incident.

Shantytown sits a short walk and an entire economy away from the doctor's house, and a boy crosses between them without noticing that he is crossing anything. Skippy takes as its emergency a dog and a dogcatcher, which sounds slight until the terms are read out: one child's pet is a possession the law can remove, and the other child's father can afford to make problems disappear. The film is from 1931 and does not pretend the distance between the two households is temporary, or that goodwill closes it. Norman Taurog's direction was honored by the Academy, as was the lead performance, given by a child, and the picture itself. The tone stays comic; the stakes do not, and the negotiating is left to people with no leverage at all.

Elin is bored in a way the town offers no exit from, and Agnes is in love in a way she can tell nobody about. Lukas Moodysson keeps both of them inside eighty-nine minutes of a small Swedish place where everyone's business is public and very little is available; the original title, Fucking Åmål, puts the town's name inside the complaint. What is at risk is ordinary and total — a teenager's standing among people she will go on seeing every day for years. The camera stays close, the performances are deliberately unpolished, and the comedy comes from how badly adolescents estimate one another. A Guldbagge for best film, a European Film Award, a place on FLM's list of the best Swedish films: a quantity of institutional agreement about two girls in a bedroom.

The teenagers are happy; the film keeps cutting away to the adults, who are not. Two hours of 1970 Sweden, and the attachment at the center is genuine enough — first love conducted with complete absorption and no curiosity about anything outside itself — but it has been mounted inside a wider family where grown people drink, work, and fail to say what is wrong. The comedy and the grief are one fact: nobody young notices, and nobody older can explain. Roy Andersson took the Guldbagge for best film with it, the country sent it to the Academy Awards, and FLM later placed it among the best Swedish films. What holds the halves together is patience, the same attention given to a courtship and to the adults nobody in the film is asking after.

The victim is a policeman, and the inquiry into his death turns almost at once into an inquiry into his conduct. Bo Widerberg films procedure rather than thrill: statements, files, a department reading its own paperwork with mounting discomfort. The premise commits the picture to something awkward for a crime thriller — the killing is the pretext, the institution is the subject, and Martin Beck's colleagues are also his material. At a hundred and eight minutes it moves without detours. Guldbagge awards went to the film and to its lead performance, Sweden sent it to the Academy Awards, and it sits on FLM's list of the best Swedish films. The difficulty is less the identity of a killer than how much of the answer anyone at the station wants to hear.

Half of the film is a staged fiction, and it makes no effort to hide the seam. Anna Odell convenes a twentieth high school reunion, lets one guest say out loud what was done to her in school, and watches a room of adults reassemble the ranking they held back then. Then the ground shifts: the second half turns on what the first half actually was, and on who was performing. Eighty-eight minutes, and the structure is the argument — a hierarchy that took years to build can be restored over drinks in about ten minutes, with everyone present cooperating. It appears on FLM's list of the best Swedish films. The uncomfortable part is not the accusation but the manners, how politely a group closes ranks when one of its members raises the past.

The word efficiencies does a great deal of work in this film, and none of it on behalf of the people on the line. A young woman who came to Sweden from Eastern Europe is good at her factory job and is told the job no longer exists; what follows is not a protest but a search for the next one, slower and much harder to dramatize. It won the European Film Award for European Discovery of the Year and went out as Sweden's submission to the Academy Awards. It sits, too, on FLM's list of the best Swedish films. Gabriela Pichler stays close, lets the workplace sound like itself, and treats a layoff as the administrative event it is delivered as. The stakes are small and exact: a wage, a household, and the indignity of being retrained for work that is not there.
